evidence.notes: Exomologesis — one post-baptismal repentance through public confession

passage.excerpt: Paraphrase: Tertullian teaches that after baptism, God has provided one further repentance (exomologesis) for those who fall into grave sin. This second repentance is a painful public confession before the congregation, including fasting, weeping, and prostration; it is the last remaining refuge for the sinner, but it does exist.
passage.notes: One post-baptismal repentance allowed through exomologesis (public confession); early penitential discipline

passage.excerpt: Paraphrase: Zephyrinus was an ignorant and illiterate individual, and one unskilled in the definitions of the Church. Callistus, who was crafty in dealing with evil, and versed in knavery, urged Zephyrinus on, and taught him that the Father and Son are the same. object_entity.notes: Hippolytus set himself up as rival bishop of Rome c. 217 after the election of Callistus I, whom he accused of modalism and moral laxity; sometimes called the first antipope; the schism persisted through the pontificates of Urban I and Pontian until reconciliation in Sardinian exile c. 235.

context_place.notes: Imperial capital associated with the Roman church and Paul later ministry.

passage.excerpt: Paraphrase: Callistus, having been appointed over the cemetery by Zephyrinus, brought many into his following. He was the first to invent the device of conniving at the sensual pleasures of men, saying that all men had their sins forgiven by himself. For he even permitted women of rank, if they were unmarried and burned with lust, to have a companion of the rank of slave or freedman.
passage.notes: Hippolytus attacks Callistus for moral laxity; permitting marriages between social classes; forgiving grave sins

subject_entity.notes: Tertullian's treatise c. 206-212 defending the literal bodily resurrection of the flesh against Gnostic spiritualizers.

object_entity.notes: First major Latin Christian author; active in Carthage c. 195–220. Wrote at least 31 works spanning apologetics, anti-heretical polemic, and moral discipline. Coined 'trinitas' and 'tres personae una substantia'. Defender of apostolic succession, rule of faith, incarnation, and bodily resurrection. Later attracted to Montanist rigorism c. 207; teacher of Cyprian by doctrinal influence.

passage.excerpt: The resurrection of the dead is the Christian's trust. By believing it we are what we claim to be. It is the truth which compels faith. And the truth God reveals. But the vulgar, and especially the heretics, disparage the resurrection.
passage.notes: Bodily resurrection as central Christian identity; truth revealed by God; against heretical deniers

subject_entity.notes: Tertullian's treatise c. 211 on whether a Christian soldier may wear a military crown; argues that military service is incompatible with Christian faith due to idolatry and bloodshed.

object_entity.notes: First major Latin Christian author; active in Carthage c. 195–220. Wrote at least 31 works spanning apologetics, anti-heretical polemic, and moral discipline. Coined 'trinitas' and 'tres personae una substantia'. Defender of apostolic succession, rule of faith, incarnation, and bodily resurrection. Later attracted to Montanist rigorism c. 207; teacher of Cyprian by doctrinal influence.

passage.excerpt: Shall it be held lawful to make an occupation of the sword, when the Lord proclaims that he who uses the sword shall perish by the sword? And shall the son of peace take part in the battle when it does not become him even to sue at law? Shall he apply the chain, and the prison, and the torture, and the punishment, who is not the avenger even of his own wrongs? Shall he stand guard for others more than for Christ? Do we believe it lawful for a human oath to be superadded to one divine?
passage.notes: Christians must not serve in the military; incompatibility of military oath, sword, and punishment with Christian faith
